ety.text: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *Bogъdanъ. Compare typologically Фёдор (Fjódor), Дорофе́й (Doroféj).

s.g: to skid, to spin around without traction (of a car or its wheels)
to stall, to be in a gridlock
x: Что́-то должно́ помога́ть, когда́ буксу́ет иро́ния На́до найти́ э́то «что́-то» и вколоти́ть э́то «что́-то» в штаке́т

ety.text: Uncertain: * бу́кса (búksa, “metal box in which a train axle rotates and into which oil is poured”) + -ова́ть (-ovátʹ). * From Polish buksować, further from Dutch boegseren, whence also букси́ровать (buksírovatʹ), букси́р (buksír).
Borrowed from Japanese 武士道 (ぶしどう, bushidō).

s.g: altitude, elevation, height above sea level

ety.text: Clipped compound of гла́вный геро́й (glávnyj gerój).
From ки́рза (kírza) + -овый (-ovyj) (stem-stressed version) or from кирза́ (kirzá) + -о́вый (-óvyj) (suffix-stressed version).

s.g: bony, gaunt (of a body: very thin, with visible bones under the skin)
high-rise (tall building, one consisting of many storeys)
foresight, sight (of a rifle or a similar weapon)

ety.text: Uncertain: * From Slavic, akin to Polish narta, Old Czech nárt, Upper Sorbian narć. * Borrowed from a Uralic language.
From не- (ne-) + завершённый (zaveršónnyj). Compare Ukrainian незаве́ршений (nezavéršenyj), Belarusian незаве́ршаны (njezavjéršany), Bulgarian незавършен (nezavăršen).
Clipped compound of областна́я администра́ция (oblastnája administrácija, “oblast administration”). Compare Ukrainian обладміністра́ція (obladministrácija).

Inherited from Middle Russian оболочка (oboločka), from оболочити (oboločiti) + -ка (-ka) or from Proto-Slavic *obvolčьka, from *obvolka + *-ьka, from *obelťi, from *ob- + *velťi. Cognate with Polish obłóczka. Compare typologically German Bezug (< ziehen << Proto-Germanic *teuhaną < Proto-Indo-European *dewk-), the term also functions as a suffix meaning case or cover, as in Kopfkissenbezug (compare на́волочка (návoločka), Polish powłoczka).

s.g: ready for defense, prepared for defense; defensible

ety.text: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *poltьnьce. By surface analysis, полотно́ (polotnó, “canvas”) + -це (-ce). Compare Old Church Slavonic платьньце (platĭnĭce) and Sanskrit पट (paṭa, “cloth, garment”).

s.g: to govern, to rule (usually of a lord or monarch)

ety.text: Inherited from Old East Slavic правити (praviti), from Proto-Slavic *praviti. By surface analysis, пра́вый (právyj) + -ить (-itʹ).

s.g: to lay in store, to lay up, to prepare, to provide

x: Он кивну́л на пуленепробива́емое окно́, за кото́рым на пло́щади у па́мятника Ива́ну III пестре́ла толпа́ демонстра́нтов.

ety.text: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sьrpъ. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic срьпъ (srĭpŭ, “sickle”), Bulgarian сърп (sărp), Czech srp, Polish sierp, Yiddish סערפּ (serp); and with Latvian sirpis, Greek ἅρπη (árpi), Latin sarpō.

s.g: to be sparing with, to be stingy with, to skimp on, to scrimp on
to save (to write a file to a disk)

x: Мединский сохранил пост министра культуры в новом правительстве.

to slurp (drink or eat (liquid food) noisily)

ety.text: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sьrbati, from Proto-Indo-European *srebʰ-. Cognate with English slurp.
Attested at least since 1780s, akin to later attested Russian тушкан (tuškan), from Kazakh тышқан (tıšqan, “mouse”), from Proto-Turkic *sïčgan.
From the Ukrainian phrase Украї́на це Євро́па (Ukrajína ce Jevrópa, “Ukraine is Europe”).
